summary:
Assam stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

State welfare machinery in Assam is thin. A reply from the Press Information Bureau to Parliament in December 2021 listed the twelve states and union territories that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under the 2019 Rules, and Assam was not among them, so no state-level board was operating there as of that date. Assam therefore has no welfare board of the kind running in other Indian states.

The complaint system in Assam is reachable but under-used. A Queerbeat crime-data report of 30 January 2026 records that two of the seven cases registered nationally under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 fell in Assam, and none in the 2023 tally. The same report cautions that national counts are very small — twenty cases across 2019 to 2023 — because police registration of complaints is biased downward, so low figures do not indicate low incidence. Its 2025 survey puts prevalence of violence against trans people at 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual.

Assam-specific experience of custody is documented: transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in the state have recounted degrading treatment. Assessment of police conduct in India more broadly is contested. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.

Entry and documentation remain a friction point across India. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities, and in November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024, when replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Sanhita removed gender-identity-specific sexual-offence safeguards that had protected trans persons. Discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have read to cover gender identity, but there is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership.
tangentialFactors:
Facilities and care access in India are set largely at state level, and Assam sits outside the leading group. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating. Intersex minors remain at risk, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

Credibility of official counts should be weighed against registration bias. The 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence recorded in the 2025 survey sits far above the twenty Transgender Persons Act cases registered nationally between 2019 and 2023.
localsOnly:
Residents of Assam had no state Transgender Welfare Board as of December 2021, when the national government listed the twelve states and union territories that had constituted one under the 2019 Rules. Welfare benefits administered through such boards elsewhere in India — housing subsidies, pensions, surgery in public hospitals — were not available through that route in Assam.

Local registration of complaints under the Transgender Persons Act is possible: Assam accounted for two of the seven cases registered nationally in 2021, and zero in 2023. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have reported degrading treatment in custody.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not establish whether Assam constituted a Transgender Welfare Board after December 2021; the only dated finding is the December 2021 list on which it was absent. Any later change is unresolved.

The inventory gives no Assam-specific figures on hate-crime offences, police complaint outcomes, or the effect of the March 2026 amendment on recognition applications in the state. The two Assam rows in the crime-data report are national Act totals, not a measure of incidence in the state.

No source here addresses same-sex marriage recognition, partner benefits, or bathroom and facilities rules as they apply within Assam, and no Assam-specific court judgment on gender-marker documents is recorded.
